title: KV cache kept as tokens; idle tensor cores recompute it
idea: IFR: the KV cache costs zero bytes. Closest achievable: store only token IDs plus a residual-stream checkpoint every 8th layer; during memory-bound decode the otherwise idle tensor cores re-derive K/V for the seven intervening layers block by block, overlapped with the weight fetch.
why: Attacks HBM capacity and the HBM TSV tax (facts 5, 6): KV footprint down ~6-8x for ~15-25% extra FLOPs that decode leaves unused anyway.

title: Price-indexed scheduler decides park versus re-prefill for idle sessions
idea: IFR: idle conversations hold no memory yet resume instantly. Closest: the serving scheduler compares each parked session's KV cost (GB x expected idle seconds x spot DRAM $/GB-s) with the FLOP cost of re-prefilling from text, using a learned per-user think-time distribution, and evicts to text or flash whenever re-prefill is cheaper.
why: 30-60% of inference KV belongs to sessions idle between turns; with DRAM at 4x price this cuts provisioned KV DRAM ~2x by turning abundant compute into memory.

title: Rack-wide content-addressed page pool for weights and libraries
idea: IFR: each distinct byte exists once per rack. Closest: a CXL memory pool indexes immutable 2 MB pages (model weights, container layers, shared libraries, JIT code) by 128-bit hash; every host maps them read-only through a small local cache, with copy-on-write on modification.
why: Inference racks replicate 70-400 GB of identical weights per server; 8-16 hosts sharing one copy recovers 40-70% of rack weight DRAM.

title: Birth-tiering allocator places objects by predicted lifetime and heat
idea: IFR: DRAM holds only bytes about to be touched. Closest: allocation call-site, type and stack-hash features feed a tiny on-CPU model that predicts each object's heat; predicted-cold objects are born directly in CXL or flash-backed memory and never migrate, so hot and cold objects never share a page.
why: Page-granular tiering strands 30-50% of near DRAM on mixed hot/cold pages; object-level birth placement cuts near DRAM 30-40%.

title: Lossless rANS-coded weights decoded inside the HBM base die
idea: IFR: weights are stored at their true information content. Closest: BF16/FP8 exponents (about 2.6 bits of entropy in 8) and top mantissa bits are rANS-coded per tensor, and line-rate decoders in the HBM/LPDDR logic die expand them so the host sees ordinary BF16.
why: ~30% lossless capacity and bandwidth gain on all weight memory with zero accuracy change; directly shrinks the HBM stacks needed per model.

title: Two-layer DRAM window streams weights from parallel flash channels
idea: IFR: weights need no DRAM residency. Closest: weights live across 16-64 NVMe/low-latency flash channels and stream layer by layer into a double buffer holding exactly two layers; the batch grows until per-layer compute hides the flash read time.
why: Weight DRAM falls by L/2 (40-60x for 80-120-layer models) for offline inference and fine-tuning; flash costs ~1/20 per bit.

title: Weight carousel rotates model shards around an accelerator ring
idea: IFR: one copy of the weights serves every chip at once. Closest: N accelerators each hold 1/N of the weights and continuously pass shards around the ring over chip-to-chip links; each chip applies the passing shard to its own batch, so the ring stores weights once instead of N times.
why: N-fold cut in replicated weight memory for data-parallel serving (8x on an 8-chip ring), paid for with link bandwidth that consumes no DRAM wafers.

title: Regenerable pages: kernel drops pages tagged with rebuild functions
idea: IFR: memory holds only information that cannot be rebuilt. Closest: applications tag pages with a regenerator (re-decode image, re-decompress file, re-JIT, rebuild index) plus a cost hint; under pressure the kernel discards them like clean page cache and a userfaultfd handler rematerializes them on fault.
why: 15-30% of client and server RSS is derived data; reclaims it with no swap I/O and no new hardware.

title: Hot-field arenas: garbage collector splits objects so rows carry hot bytes
idea: IFR: every fetched byte gets used. Closest: a managed runtime profiles per-field access and, during compaction, moves hot fields into dense hot arenas in near DRAM and cold fields into a far-memory arena reached by a compressed offset.
why: Objects average 20-40% hot fields; near-tier footprint drops 1.5-2x and row overfetch (fact 8) falls with it.

title: Revocable leases sell stranded VM memory to caches and batch jobs
idea: IFR: no installed DRAM bit is ever idle. Closest: hypervisors lease allocated-but-untouched guest memory (30-50% in public clouds) to caches and batch jobs under a 50 ms revocation contract; leased contents must be regenerable, so revocation simply drops them.
why: Recovers 20-40% of fleet DRAM with zero new chips.

title: Transformer prefetcher in CXL controller makes flash act like DRAM
idea: IFR: infinite capacity at DRAM speed via a perfect oracle. Closest: a CXL expander fronting SLC NAND with a 5% DRAM cache runs an on-controller sequence model trained on each tenant's miss stream (page deltas plus PC hints sent over CXL), issuing prefetches 50-100 us ahead.
why: 4-8x less DRAM for graph analytics and recommendation at under 15% slowdown once hit rate exceeds 99%.

title: Bit-plane storage with learned LSB synthesis on read
idea: IFR: store only the bits that matter. Closest: error-tolerant arrays (activations, images, sensor data) are stored as bit planes, MSB planes in DRAM and LSB planes dropped or parked in flash; on read a tiny predictor in the memory controller synthesizes dithered LSBs from neighbouring values within a programmer-declared SNR budget.
why: 1.5-2.5x capacity for media and ML activations at controlled error.

title: Frozen foundation models burned into via-programmed ROM
idea: IFR: weights use no DRAM because they are the hardware. Closest: for models frozen for years (speech, embedding, vision encoders) weights are encoded by one custom via mask as ROM beside the MACs at ~0.1 um2/bit, with LoRA adapters in SRAM for updates.
why: Removes 70-90% of inference DRAM for frozen models; ROM needs no capacitor, no refresh and only one non-EUV custom mask.

title: KV cache as inverted-file vector index with DRAM-resident centroids
idea: IFR: context length is free. Closest: KV blocks are clustered online into an IVF index stored in flash; DRAM holds only the centroids and a recent window, and each decode query fetches its top-k clusters for sparse attention.
why: DRAM per million-token context falls 20-50x with ~1% quality loss on retrieval-heavy tasks.

title: Sub-page MMU mapping merges sparse pages into one frame
idea: IFR: zero fragmentation. Closest: the MMU gains a 256 B mesh granularity inside 4 KB pages so two half-empty pages whose live slots do not overlap share one physical frame; a hardware bitmap scanner finds mergeable pairs.
why: Fragmentation wastes 10-30% of heap DRAM in long-running servers (Redis, browsers, JVMs); most of it is reclaimed.

title: Hardware concurrent garbage collector lets heaps run near live size
idea: IFR: managed heaps equal their live set. Closest: a GC engine in the memory controller marks and compacts concurrently, with read-barrier forwarding checks in the load path, so runtimes run at 1.1-1.2x live set instead of the 2-3x headroom software GC needs.
why: Java/Go/.NET heaps are a large share of server DRAM and 40-60% of it is headroom; that headroom is removed.

title: Prediction-residual codec for simulation fields and time series
idea: IFR: memory stores only surprise. Closest: a memory-controller codec stores HPC fields and telemetry as entropy-coded residuals from a predictor (previous timestep, neighbour stencil), like video P-frames, decoded losslessly on access.
why: 3-10x footprint reduction for smooth physical fields in climate, CFD and sensor workloads.

title: DRAM-less SSDs via learned-index flash translation held in host
idea: IFR: storage needs no DRAM. Closest: host-managed/zoned SSDs whose logical-to-physical map is a piecewise-linear learned index 50-100x smaller than a page-level FTL table, kept in host DRAM, so SSD controllers ship without their ~1 GB/TB DRAM.
why: SSD-embedded DRAM is several percent of global DRAM bits; deleting most of it frees that supply for compute.

title: Router-lookahead prefetch pages MoE experts from flash
idea: IFR: only the experts this token uses occupy memory. Closest: a small predictor reads layer-i hidden states to guess the top experts for layers i+1 to i+3 and prefetches them from flash into an expert cache; a miss falls back to the always-resident shared expert for that token.
why: Large MoE serving keeps only 10-20% expert residency, cutting DRAM 5-8x.

title: Compiler swaps pointer structures for succinct ones with rank/select instructions
idea: IFR: indexes sized at the information-theoretic minimum. Closest: a profile-guided compiler pass replaces read-mostly maps, sets and trees with succinct equivalents (Elias-Fano, wavelet trees, compressed tries) backed by new rank/select instructions.
why: 2-5x footprint cut for indexes and graphs in search, ads and genomics.

title: Scheduler pairs jobs with anticorrelated memory peaks on shared slabs
idea: IFR: memory sized for total use, not for the sum of peaks. Closest: a cluster scheduler profiles each job's memory time series and co-locates anticorrelated pairs (checkpointing training vs diurnal inference, ETL vs serving) on one pooled DRAM slab with priority preemption to compressed swap.
why: Cuts provisioned DRAM 20-35% versus peak-sized allocation.

title: Superposed tensor storage with random-sign binding keys
idea: IFR: one buffer holds many tensors at once. Closest: k low-precision tensors (e.g., gradient accumulators of k micro-batches or k LoRA deltas) are each multiplied by a random +/-1 key vector and summed into one buffer; unbinding with the same key recovers each one with noise that error-tolerant training absorbs.
why: k-fold (k~4-8) memory cut for noise-tolerant accumulators; a hyperdimensional-computing trade of noise for capacity.

title: Load-and-kill instruction frees memory at a value's last use
idea: IFR: memory frees itself the instant data is dead. Closest: a compiler-emitted load-and-kill instruction marks a line or page dead after its final read; the cache drops it without writeback and the OS reclaims fully dead frames immediately.
why: Cuts temporary-buffer footprint 10-20% in streaming and ML pipelines and removes useless writeback bandwidth.

title: Seed-generated weights from LFSR banks in mature-node logic
idea: IFR: weights that occupy no memory. Constraint: memory chips need W, Hf and Ta but plain logic need not, so trade memory for logic: each 8x8 weight block is stored as a 16-bit LFSR seed plus four small coefficients, and thousands of LFSR+MAC units regenerate weights at line rate in 65-130 nm CMOS wired in Al-Cu with Ti/TiN barriers and TiSi2 contacts.
why: ~3-4 bits per weight cuts weight DRAM 4-5x versus BF16 using only Si, Al, Cu, Ti, N and O.

title: Host-DRAM-lite AI servers decode data shards directly on GPU
idea: IFR: AI-server host memory shrinks to almost nothing. Constraint: adding no new chips means adding no scarce elements, so delete host DRAM's jobs instead: compressed training shards go storage-to-GPU and are decoded by GPU kernels, and checkpoints stream GPU-to-NVMe directly, removing the staging buffers that justify 1-2 TB per node.
why: Host DRAM per AI node drops from ~2 TB to ~256 GB, an 8x cut on a large slice of server DRAM bought today.

title: SONOS NOR arrays compute dense layers where the weights sit
idea: IFR: weights never move and never occupy DRAM. Closest within Si/O/N: poly-Si/SiO2/Si3N4/SiO2 charge-trap NOR arrays (no Hf, W or Ta; Ti-silicide contacts) store 4-bit weights as trapped charge and do analog multiply-accumulate by summing bitline currents; only activations and KV use DRAM.
why: Removes weight DRAM (50-80% of inference memory) with a three-element memory stack mature U.S. fabs already run.

title: TiO2 crossbars hold recommendation embedding tables with in-array gather
idea: IFR: terabyte embedding tables cost nothing. Closest with abundant elements: Ti/TiO2-x/Ti resistive crossbars (no Hf or Ta oxide) store read-mostly embedding rows rewritten monthly (endurance need ~100 cycles), and an in-array gather-sum pools the looked-up rows before anything crosses to DRAM.
why: Embedding tables dominate recommender DRAM at TB scale; displaces 80-90% of it.

title: Carbon antifuse ROM executes OS and library code in place
idea: IFR: immutable software consumes no RAM. Closest with C, H, Al and Si only: a one-time-programmable crossbar where a-C:H films between Al lines are fused into sp2 filaments by current pulses; each OS release, runtime and standard library is burned once and mapped execute-in-place, so code pages never occupy DRAM.
why: Code and read-only data are 5-15% of RSS on servers and phones; removed from DRAM for pennies of carbon.

title: Tungsten-free 3D NAND with silicided-poly wordlines as KV overflow tier
idea: IFR: unlimited KV overflow with no chokepoint materials. Closest: 3D charge-trap NAND built with TiSi2-clad doped poly-Si wordlines instead of W replacement gates, accepting higher wordline RC through shorter blocks, read in large sequential KV pages behind a small DRAM cache.
why: Makes the DRAM-offload tier itself W-free while enabling ~10x less DRAM for long-context serving.

title: Laser-free rack memory pool over a passive copper backplane
idea: IFR: memory follows demand anywhere. Constraint: optical links need GaAs/InP lasers and InGaAs detectors (Ga, In), so stay electrical: a 1.5 m passive Cu twinax backplane and mature-node CXL switches with Al-Cu/Ti wiring pool DRAM across 16-32 hosts, sized to the P99 of the aggregate rather than each host's peak.
why: 20-30% less DRAM per rack with zero III-V parts.

title: DRAM-free inference pipeline across hundreds of mature-node SRAM chips
idea: IFR: no DRAM at all. Closest using only Si, Al, Cu, Ti, N and O: partition a model layer by layer across many 40-65 nm SRAM-heavy chips (TiSi2 contacts, Ti-barrier Cu, SiON/poly gates, no high-k metal gate) so every weight sits in SRAM beside its MAC, and pipeline large batches through the chain.
why: Eliminates weight DRAM entirely using idle mature-node U.S. capacity; higher cost per bit but no EUV and no scarce elements.

title: In/Ga-free zinc-silicon-oxide gain cells stacked over accelerator logic
idea: IFR: the KV cache lives on the compute die for free. The constraint bans IGZO, so use amorphous Zn-Si-O channels: 2T0C gain cells deposited below 400 C in the BEOL above the attention units, with TiN electrodes and Al2O3 gate dielectric, holding transient KV and activations for milliseconds with occasional refresh.
why: Moves the hot KV set off external HBM; if ZSO leakage approaches IGZO's, refresh becomes negligible and several GB sit on-die.

title: Bump-in-the-wire compression ASIC built in 130 nm aluminium fabs
idea: IFR: every DRAM chip holds twice its bits for free. Closest within the constraint: an inline CXL/DIMM LZ-class compressor plus zero-line elider fabbed on 130 nm Al-interconnect lines (Ti/TiN barriers, TiSi2 contacts, no W plugs, no Hf); the OS overcommits physical memory 2x with backpressure when compressibility drops.
why: 2-3x effective capacity per DRAM bit on typical server data, made in idle U.S. mature fabs.

title: Compiler region inference sizes heaps to the exact peak live set
idea: IFR: programs allocate exactly what they use at each instant. The constraint pushes to zero new hardware: a whole-program region-inference compiler (lifetime analysis in the style of Rust/MLKit) assigns every allocation to a stack-like region freed in bulk, removing allocator slack, fragmentation and GC headroom.
why: Cuts footprint 25-50% for allocation-heavy services with zero materials of any kind.

title: Count-sketch compressed Adam moments for large-model training
idea: IFR: optimizer state takes no memory. Closest without new chips: Adam's first and second moments live in a count-sketch with heavy-hitter correction; exact moments are kept only for the top 1% of parameters by gradient magnitude, the rest use sketched estimates.
why: Optimizer state is 8-12 bytes per parameter; sketching cuts training DRAM/HBM 2-3x for large models.

title: Superword tokenizer halves tokens and halves KV per conversation
idea: IFR: a whole thought fits in one KV slot. Closest with no hardware: retrain tokenizers with ~1M-entry multi-word vocabularies (frequent phrases as single tokens), moving cost into a larger embedding table that is stored once while every live sequence carries ~2x fewer tokens.
why: KV memory scales with token count; ~40-50% KV cut fleet-wide for a one-time embedding cost.

title: Retrofit latent KV into existing models via SVD and brief finetune
idea: IFR: each token's KV is a few dozen numbers. Closest without new silicon: factor each layer's K/V projections by SVD into a shared low-rank latent (MLA-style), cache only the latent, absorb the up-projection into the query and output matrices, then heal with a short distillation finetune.
why: 4-8x KV reduction on already-trained MHA/GQA models without full retraining.

title: Gist tokens compress long system prompts into cached soft vectors
idea: IFR: shared instructions cost nothing per user. Closest with no materials: a trained compressor distills each long system prompt or document into 16-64 learned gist tokens, so every session caches the gist KV instead of thousands of prompt tokens.
why: System and RAG prompts are often 50-80% of per-session KV; 20-100x compression on that portion.

title: Retired DDR4 reborn in CXL expanders as compressed far tier
idea: IFR: memory already mined is used forever. Constraint: no new extraction of W, Hf or Ta, so harvest DDR4 DIMMs from decommissioned servers, test and bin them, and mount them in CXL type-3 expanders behind an inline compressor as a far tier for cold pages.
why: Turns a waste stream into usable capacity, offsetting 20-30% of new DDR5 purchases in a refresh cycle with zero new scarce elements.

title: On-sensor tokenizers so raw frames never land in DRAM
idea: IFR: perception data enters memory already understood. Closest in plain Si CMOS: stacked image sensors with a small patch-embedding network in the logic layer emit compact tokens or event deltas instead of raw frames, so camera pipelines skip multi-frame DRAM buffers.
why: Cuts frame-buffer DRAM 10-50x in phones, cars and robots, and removes the matching DRAM traffic.

title: Tax credit for certified bytes-per-task software reductions
idea: IFR: saving a byte is valued like making one. Constraint: no materials at all, so make it policy: a federal credit pays firms per GB-year of DRAM demand avoided, measured against a standardized bytes-per-task benchmark suite and audited like energy-efficiency incentives.
why: Creates a market for compression, dedup and KV-efficiency software; a 10% demand cut equals a fab's output without the $15B.

title: Hardware interning engine stores each string or record once
idea: IFR: every distinct value exists once. Closest with mature-node Al/Ti logic: a memory-side engine hash-conses immutable strings, JSON nodes and tuples at allocation, returning a refcounted handle to an existing copy, with 64-bit hash probes done near memory.
why: String and record duplication is 10-30% of heap in web, log and analytics services.

title: Hybrid state-space retrofit replaces most attention layers' KV
idea: IFR: context costs constant memory. Closest with no new hardware: replace 7 of every 8 attention layers in a trained model with linear-recurrent state-space layers (fixed-size state) distilled from the originals, keeping one attention layer in eight for exact recall.
why: ~8x KV reduction for long contexts at modest quality cost.

title: Datacenter-wide prefix radix tree deduplicates shared KV across users
idea: IFR: identical context is cached once for the planet. Closest with no materials: a cluster-wide radix tree keyed by token prefixes stores shared KV blocks (system prompts, popular documents, few-shot examples) once per pod, and requests are routed to the pod holding their longest prefix.
why: Shared prefixes are 30-70% of tokens in many products; that share of KV is deduplicated.

title: Glass-interposer LPDDR fan-out replaces HBM stacks
idea: IFR: bandwidth without the TSV tax. The constraint drives toward Si/Al/O/Na/Ca glass: aluminosilicate glass interposers with fine Cu/Ti redistribution wiring fan out 16-32 standard LPDDR dies around the accelerator at wide I/O, with no TSVs and no Ta barriers.
why: HBM uses ~3x the wafer area per bit of DDR (fact 6); delivering similar capacity with planar LPDDR needs about one third of the DRAM wafers.

title: Cascade router sends easy queries to small models first
idea: IFR: every query is answered with the smallest memory possible. Closest with no hardware: a confidence-calibrated cascade routes queries to a 3B model (6 GB) first and escalates to the 400B model only when a verifier flags uncertainty, so fewer replicas of the giant model are needed.
why: If 70% of traffic stays small, giant-model replicas and their HBM drop ~3x.
